A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and are readable throughout. v1 ends after the references despite citing appendices; v2 supplies Appendices A–F. Their inclusion can be assessed as added documentation without assuming that every documented experiment was newly conducted.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original simulation results, fitted benchmark rankings, and an in-house subsampling study, distinct from externally sourced benchmark scores.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and reports additional mixed-quality judge, tie-handling, question-length, and sparse-graph analyses.

M1.justification: The main scalar-discrimination BTL model and projected Adam procedure remain. Appendix F.6 adds an optional extension with gamma_k(z) = exp(alpha_k + beta_k z), using standardized question length and additional per-judge slope parameters with row-level gradients.

E1.justification: The benchmark inventory remains MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and the in-house dataset. Appendix F.7 extends the tested input conditions to deliberately restricted connected comparison graphs, including a spanning-tree regime, without adding a new application domain.

E2.justification: Unweighted BTL remains the principal baseline. Appendix F.6 adds a direct internal comparison between the scalar model and its length-dependent extension. REM, GTR, and FTR remain discussed rather than empirically benchmarked.

E3.justification: New protocols include a six-lower/two-higher-quality judge pool assessed against a common weighted reference, tie-removal refits, and fixed-budget graph thinning (Section 5.4; Appendices F.4 and F.7). Appendix C.2 also describes spanning-tree seeding, qualifying v1's uniform-sampling account; the PDFs do not establish that retained simulations were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of mixed judge quality, sensitivity to removing ties, length-dependent discrimination, and sparse comparison graphs. Appendices F.2 and F.5 additionally examine rank-based sample efficiency and judge discrimination across model sizes and datasets, extending v1's reported simulation, efficiency, and case-study evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 repetitions with interquartile bands for MSE, 500 replications for coverage, five repetitions for subsampling, and Wald confidence intervals. Additional interval rows and covariance derivations do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: The main benchmark tables and Figures 1–4 retain their results. New Section 5.4 reports weighted versus unweighted Pearson correlations of 0.9394 versus 0.8992 and Spearman correlations of 0.9212 versus 0.8316. Appendices add full rankings, judge estimates, tie-removal results, length-extension rank correlation of 0.9996, and sparse-graph results. These are additional findings, not improvements to retained same-setting scores.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces uniform sampling with general full-support sampling and explicitly adds compact localization to Theorem 3.4. Appendix A supplies previously absent proofs and covariance derivations. Appendix F.6 adds an identifiability theorem and normalization corollary for the length-dependent extension.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions remain substantially unchanged. The conclusion narrows 'consistently outperforms' to demonstrating empirical improvements and describes estimation of judge discrimination rather than unrestricted judge reliability. The introduction adds emphasis on gains with mixed-quality judge pools.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes discrimination relative to the learned ranking from objective correctness. It adds substantive limitations concerning correlated judge errors, shared biases, and imbalanced or adaptive comparison designs. Appendix F.6 qualifies length effects as potentially confounded, while F.2 discusses the trade-off between judge diversity and comparisons per judge.

D1.justification: Previously referenced but absent appendices now provide algorithm pseudocode, gradients, simulation budgets and parameter construction, dataset counts, judge identities, decoding settings, and the complete judge prompt. v2 also identifies the excluded near-zero-discrimination judge and supplies a code/data access link. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to all underlying settings.

R1.justification: v2 adds Newey and McFadden (1994) for the estimation proofs and explicitly contrasts FTR's overlapping judge/candidate pools with its own unrestricted pools. Other prominent reference changes are publication-metadata updates to already cited works.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local revisions clarify discrimination and estimation terminology, expand the conclusion, insert the judge-heterogeneity subsection, and add acknowledgments and an impact statement. The extensive supplementary scientific additions do not constitute a wholesale rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds a main-text judge-scale table and substantial appendix displays: comparison heatmaps, a prompt template, full ranking tables, judge-discrimination plots, length-response curves, and sparse-graph results. The original four figures and benchmark tables remain, with relocation, reflow, and Chatbot Arena table renumbering.

improvement.justification: v1 deferred essential proofs and implementation details to appendices absent from the supplied PDF. v2 supplies that material, states important theoretical conditions, and adds targeted robustness evidence and substantive interpretive limits, substantially improving assessability and reproducibility. The gains are qualified by the mixed-quality study's internally fitted reference and the unresolved uniform-sampling versus spanning-tree description, but these limitations do not outweigh the improvements.
